Between approximately 1778 and 1871, the United States entered into over 370 ratified treaties with Indigenous nations. These were not informal understandings or suggestions. They were binding legal instruments negotiated between sovereign entities, ratified by the United States Senate, and signed by presidents. They carried—and continue to carry—the full weight of federal law.

The vast majority of these treaties contained specific provisions recognizing Indigenous land rights, establishing defined territorial boundaries, and guaranteeing that remaining lands would be held by tribes in perpetuity. The Treaty of Fort Laramie (1851 and 1868), for instance, recognized the Great Sioux Nation's sovereignty over a vast territory encompassing much of present-day South Dakota, Wyoming, Montana, and Nebraska. The treaties with the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole nations guaranteed specific territorial holdings in exchange for the devastating concession of ancestral homelands in the Southeast.

Systematic Violation

Virtually every one of these treaties was subsequently violated by the United States government—not incidentally, not accidentally, but as a matter of deliberate policy. The pattern was consistent: the government would negotiate a treaty recognizing Indigenous territorial rights, and then, when settlers, mining interests, railroad companies, or military strategists demanded access to those lands, the government would unilaterally abrogate or reinterpret the treaty, reduce the guaranteed territory, or simply ignore the agreement altogether.

The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie is perhaps the most legally significant example. It guaranteed the Black Hills (Paha Sapa) to the Lakota people "in perpetuity." When gold was discovered in the Black Hills in 1874, the federal government first attempted to purchase the land. When the Lakota refused, the government sent military forces—including George Armstrong Custer's Seventh Cavalry—to seize it. After the Great Sioux War of 1876–77, Congress passed a statute in 1877 confiscating the Black Hills without the consent required by the treaty's own terms or by federal law.

Over a century later, the U.S. Supreme Court confirmed that this seizure was illegal. In United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians (1980), the Court ruled that the taking of the Black Hills constituted an unconstitutional violation of the Fifth Amendment and awarded $105 million in compensation. The Lakota refused the money—which has since grown to over $1.3 billion in a trust account—because they do not want payment for stolen property. They want the property itself returned. The Lakota position is not sentimental; it is the most legally coherent response to the situation. When a thief is caught with stolen goods, the remedy under law is not to allow the thief to keep the goods and pay a price of their choosing. The remedy is return.

The Legal Obligation Remains

The critical legal point is that treaty violations do not extinguish treaty rights. This principle has been repeatedly affirmed by federal courts. In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the Supreme Court recognized tribal sovereignty and the binding nature of federal-tribal treaties. In Winters v. United States (1908), the Court affirmed that treaty-reserved rights persist unless explicitly abrogated by Congress. In McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020), the Court ruled that the Muscogee (Creek) Nation's reservation, established by treaty, had never been legally disestablished, despite over a century of Oklahoma and federal government conduct premised on the assumption that it had been.

McGirt is a landmark not because it created new law, but because it insisted that existing law be followed. Justice Neil Gorsuch, writing for the majority, stated: "On the far end of the Trail of Tears was a promise." The decision held that promises made in treaties remain legally binding until Congress explicitly and clearly abrogates them—and that the mere passage of time, the settlement of non-Native populations on treaty lands, and the administrative convenience of ignoring treaties do not constitute legal disestablishment.

If courts are prepared to follow this logic—and McGirt demonstrates that at least some are—then the legal foundation for large-scale land restitution is not speculative. It is already embedded in existing precedent. The question is not whether the law supports restitution; it is whether the political system has the courage to follow the law it claims to revere.

II. The Historical Record: Seizure, Removal, and Destruction

The Scale of Dispossession

The legal case for restitution is inseparable from the historical record of how dispossession occurred. The history is not ambiguous. The methods by which the United States acquired Indigenous lands included:

Military conquest and genocide. From the colonial-era wars of extermination—such as the Pequot War (1636–38), during which English settlers burned a Pequot village and killed between 400 and 700 men, women, and children—through the Indian Wars of the nineteenth century, military force was a primary mechanism of land acquisition. The Sand Creek Massacre (1864), the Washita Massacre (1868), the Marias Massacre (1870), and the Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) were not aberrations. They were instruments of a territorial policy that understood Indigenous people as obstacles to expansion.

Forced removal. The Indian Removal Act of 1830, signed by President Andrew Jackson, authorized the forced relocation of approximately 60,000 members of the so-called "Five Civilized Tribes" from their ancestral lands in the southeastern United States to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma). The Cherokee Trail of Tears alone killed an estimated 4,000 people. This removal occurred despite the Supreme Court's ruling in Worcester v. Georgia (1832) that the Cherokee Nation was a sovereign entity whose territorial rights could not be infringed by state governments. Jackson reportedly said, "John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it"—a statement that, whether apocryphal or not, accurately captures the government's approach to Indigenous legal rights throughout its history.

Allotment and forced assimilation. The Dawes Act of 1887 was perhaps the single most destructive legislative instrument of land theft. Under the guise of "civilizing" Native Americans by transforming them into individual property owners, the Act broke up communally held tribal lands into individual allotments of 80 to 160 acres per family head. The remaining "surplus" lands—often the most valuable and arable—were opened to white settlement. Between 1887 and 1934, when the Indian Reorganization Act partially reversed the policy, Native American landholdings were reduced from approximately 138 million acres to 48 million acres—a loss of nearly two-thirds. Much of the remaining land was arid, remote, and economically unproductive. The Dawes Act was designed to destroy tribal sovereignty, communal land tenure, and Indigenous cultural practices. It succeeded in all three aims to a devastating degree.

Termination and relocation. In the mid-twentieth century, the federal government pursued a policy of "termination," unilaterally dissolving the legal status of over 100 tribes and ending federal recognition and services. Simultaneously, the Indian Relocation Act of 1956 encouraged Native Americans to leave reservations for urban areas, further severing connections to land and community. These policies resulted in additional land losses and the destruction of tribal governance structures.

Fraud and Coercion in Treaty-Making

Even treaties that were ostensibly negotiated in good faith were frequently obtained through fraud, coercion, or manipulation. The Treaty of New Echota (1835), which authorized Cherokee removal, was signed by a small unauthorized faction of Cherokee leaders and explicitly repudiated by the elected Cherokee government and the vast majority of the Cherokee people. The federal government ratified it anyway. Numerous other treaties were signed by individuals who had no authority to cede land, or were negotiated under conditions of military duress, starvation, or deception about the terms being agreed to. The notion that these transactions constituted legitimate, consensual transfers of property is a legal fiction that no honest analysis can sustain.

III. The Moral Imperative: Justice Demands Action

The Ongoing Nature of the Harm

The case for reparations is strengthened by the fact that the harm caused by land dispossession is not historical in the sense of being completed and past. It is ongoing and structural. The poverty, health crises, and social dysfunction that characterize many Native American communities are not the result of cultural deficiency or personal failure. They are the direct, traceable, and predictable consequences of deliberate policy choices made by the United States government.

Native Americans experience the highest poverty rate of any racial or ethnic group in the United States. According to U.S. Census data, approximately 25% of Native Americans live below the federal poverty line, compared to roughly 10% of white Americans. Life expectancy for Native Americans is 5.5 years lower than the national average, according to the Indian Health Service. Rates of diabetes, suicide, substance abuse, and infant mortality are dramatically higher in Native communities. The Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota—located on what remains of the Great Sioux Reservation after the illegal seizure of the Black Hills—has an unemployment rate that has historically hovered between 80% and 90%, a male life expectancy comparable to that of developing nations, and housing conditions that would be considered a humanitarian crisis if they occurred in any other context.

These conditions exist because the land base that sustained Indigenous economies, cultures, and governance systems was stolen. The resources that would have enabled Native nations to develop their own institutions, economies, and social services were extracted and transferred to non-Native settlers and corporations. The current wealth of the United States—its cities, farms, industries, infrastructure, and financial systems—is built on a foundation of Indigenous land and resources acquired through illegal and immoral means.

Corrective Justice

The philosophical case for reparations draws on established principles of corrective justice: when one party wrongfully harms another, the wrongdoer has an obligation to restore the injured party, as nearly as possible, to the position they would have occupied absent the wrong. This is not a radical principle. It is the foundation of tort law, contract law, and property law. It is the principle that governs every insurance claim, every lawsuit for damages, and every criminal restitution order in the American legal system. The only reason it is considered "radical" in the context of Native American claims is that the scale of the wrong is so enormous and the beneficiaries of the wrong are so numerous that fulfilling the obligation would require significant redistribution.

But the scale of a wrong does not diminish the obligation to remedy it. If anything, the greater the wrong, the greater the imperative for redress. The argument that restitution is impractical because so many non-Native people now live on formerly Indigenous lands is not an argument against justice—it is a description of the magnitude of the injustice. The fact that stolen property has been improved, subdivided, and sold multiple times does not extinguish the original owner's claim. It complicates the remedy, but it does not eliminate the obligation.

The Inadequacy of Money Alone

Financial reparations are a necessary but insufficient component of justice. Money can address some of the economic damage caused by dispossession, fund the rebuilding of tribal institutions, and provide resources for healthcare, education, housing, and economic development. But land is not merely an economic asset for Indigenous peoples. It is the foundation of cultural identity, spiritual practice, political sovereignty, and ecological knowledge. The relationship between Indigenous peoples and their ancestral lands is not analogous to the relationship between a homeowner and a piece of real estate. It is more fundamental—closer to the relationship between a people and their language, their history, their sense of self.

This is why the Lakota have refused the Black Hills money. This is why the slogan "Land Back" resonates so powerfully across Indian Country. Financial compensation without land return is, at best, a partial remedy that addresses symptoms while leaving the underlying injury intact. At worst, it is a mechanism for laundering theft—paying an arbitrary price to retrospectively legitimize an illegal taking.

IV. Sovereignty: The Political Foundation

Indigenous Nations as Sovereign Entities

The case for restitution is fundamentally a case about sovereignty. Indigenous nations are not ethnic minorities seeking inclusion in the American mainstream. They are sovereign political entities with inherent rights to self-governance that predate the existence of the United States. This sovereignty has been recognized—however inconsistently and inadequately—by the U.S. Constitution, by hundreds of treaties, by the Supreme Court's "Marshall Trilogy" (Johnson v. M'Intosh, 1823; Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, 1831; Worcester v. Georgia, 1832), and by subsequent federal law and policy.

But sovereignty without a land base is sovereignty in name only. A nation that does not control its own territory, resources, and economic base is a dependent entity, subject to the whims and policies of the dominant power. This is precisely the condition in which most Native American nations currently exist: formally recognized as sovereign, but practically constrained to reservation lands that are often small, fragmented, resource-poor, and subject to extensive federal oversight and control.

Land restitution is not merely an economic or moral issue. It is a political necessity for the restoration of meaningful Indigenous sovereignty. Without land, there can be no genuine self-determination. Without self-determination, there can be no true justice.

International Law and Global Precedent

The international legal framework strongly supports Indigenous land restitution. The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), adopted by the General Assembly in 2007 and belatedly endorsed by the United States in 2010, affirms Indigenous peoples' rights to the lands, territories, and resources they have traditionally owned, occupied, or used (Article 26), and their right to redress, including restitution, for lands confiscated or taken without free, prior, and informed consent (Article 28). The International Labour Organization's Convention 169 similarly recognizes Indigenous land rights and the obligation of states to provide redress for historical dispossession.

Global precedent demonstrates that land restitution is not only morally required but practically achievable. In New Zealand, the Treaty of Waitangi settlement process has resulted in billions of dollars in compensation and the return of significant land and resources to Māori iwi (tribes). In Australia, the Mabo v. Queensland (1992) decision recognized native title, leading to the return of substantial areas of land to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. In Canada, modern treaty processes and land claim agreements have transferred large areas of land and self-governance authority to First Nations and Inuit communities. In South Africa, the post-apartheid constitution established a framework for land restitution to communities dispossessed under apartheid and colonial-era laws.

None of these processes has been perfect. All have been contested, slow, and incomplete. But they demonstrate that democratic societies can grapple with historical land theft and pursue meaningful restitution without collapsing into chaos. The argument that land return is "impossible" in the American context is refuted by the experience of every other settler-colonial society that has attempted it.

V. Addressing Objections

"It Was Too Long Ago"

The most common objection to Native American restitution is temporal: that the wrongs occurred too long ago, that the perpetrators and victims are dead, and that contemporary Americans bear no responsibility for historical crimes. This objection fails on multiple grounds.

First, federal treaty violations are not merely historical events. They are ongoing legal conditions. A treaty that has been violated but never legally abrogated remains in effect. The obligation to honor it persists regardless of how much time has passed. As the Supreme Court recognized in McGirt, the passage of time does not disestablish legal rights.

Second, the harms caused by dispossession are not historical in the sense of being completed. Native American communities continue to suffer the material consequences of land theft every day, in the form of poverty, poor health, inadequate infrastructure, and limited economic opportunity. These are present harms, not merely historical grievances.

Third, the argument proves too much. If temporal distance extinguished legal and moral obligations, then no long-term debt would be enforceable, no estate could be inherited, and no nation could be held to obligations undertaken by previous administrations. The United States routinely holds other nations to treaties, agreements, and obligations entered into decades or centuries ago. It cannot simultaneously claim the right to ignore its own treaty obligations on the grounds that they are old.

Fourth, contemporary Americans continue to benefit from the land theft. Every American who owns land, pays property taxes, uses public land, or benefits from the natural resources extracted from formerly Indigenous territory is a beneficiary of dispossession. The obligation to remedy a wrong is not limited to the original wrongdoer; it extends to those who continue to benefit from the wrong.

"It's Impractical"

The objection that large-scale land return is impractical misunderstands what restitution advocates are proposing. No serious proposal calls for the forcible removal of non-Native populations from their homes. Land restitution can take many forms:

  • Return of federal public lands. The federal government controls approximately 640 million acres of land—roughly 28% of the total land area of the United States. Much of this land—national forests, Bureau of Land Management holdings, military installations—was taken from Indigenous peoples and is currently used for purposes that could be maintained under tribal management or co-management. The return of significant portions of federal land to tribal nations is entirely feasible and would not displace a single private landowner.

  • Co-management arrangements. In cases where full return is not immediately feasible, co-management agreements can restore Indigenous decision-making authority over land use, resource extraction, and environmental protection. The Bears Ears Inter-Tribal Coalition's advocacy for the Bears Ears National Monument in Utah provides a model for collaborative land management that respects both Indigenous sovereignty and broader public interests.

  • Conservation and ecological restoration. Many Indigenous nations have demonstrated superior capacity for environmental stewardship. Indigenous-managed lands have been shown to harbor greater biodiversity and store more carbon than comparable non-Indigenous lands. Land return can serve both justice and environmental sustainability goals simultaneously.

  • Purchase and transfer of private lands. Where private lands are at issue, voluntary purchase programs—funded by reparations appropriations—can facilitate the gradual return of land to tribal ownership. This approach respects existing property rights while working toward the long-term goal of restoring Indigenous land bases.

  • Urban land return. In urban areas built on former Indigenous territories, land trusts, community land models, and dedicated Indigenous spaces can provide meaningful restitution without requiring wholesale population transfer.

The practical mechanisms for land return exist. What is lacking is political will.

"Other Groups Suffered Too"

The argument that other groups have also suffered historical injustices—and therefore Native American claims should not be prioritized—is a non sequitur. The fact that other injustices exist does not diminish the obligation to remedy this one. Moreover, Native American claims are legally and structurally distinct from those of other groups. They are based on specific, identifiable treaty obligations that were violated by the federal government. They involve the dispossession of sovereign nations, not merely the mistreatment of individuals or minority groups. And they implicate the foundational legitimacy of the American state in a way that no other historical injustice does.

The United States exists on land that was taken from Indigenous peoples through processes that violated the government's own laws and treaty commitments. Addressing this fact is not in competition with addressing other injustices. It is a prerequisite for the moral coherence of any claim the United States makes about being a nation of laws.

VI. The Path Forward

What would a serious program of Native American land restitution and financial reparations look like? While the specific details would need to be negotiated between the federal government and individual tribal nations, the broad contours are clear:

  1. A comprehensive federal commission to review all treaty violations, illegal land seizures, and other acts of dispossession, and to make binding recommendations for restitution. This commission must include substantial Indigenous representation and decision-making authority.

  2. Large-scale transfer of federal public lands to tribal nations, beginning with lands that are of particular cultural, spiritual, or economic significance to specific tribes.

  3. A reparations fund of sufficient scale to address the accumulated economic damage of centuries of dispossession. Scholars have proposed various methods for calculating the appropriate sum—including the current market value of illegally seized lands, the economic value of extracted resources, and the accumulated compound interest on treaty-guaranteed payments that were never made. Any credible estimate runs into the trillions of dollars. This figure may seem staggering, but it reflects the staggering scale of what was taken.

  4. Restoration of full sovereignty over tribal lands, including jurisdiction over criminal and civil law, environmental regulation, resource management, and economic development, free from the paternalistic oversight of the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

  5. Constitutional and legislative reform to provide permanent, enforceable protections for treaty rights and tribal sovereignty, insulated from the political vagaries of changing administrations.

  6. Investment in Indigenous-led institutions—schools, healthcare systems, housing, cultural preservation programs, language revitalization—to address the accumulated damage of centuries of forced assimilation.

Conclusion

The United States has spent over two centuries building wealth, power, and institutions on a foundation of Indigenous land theft. It has done so while simultaneously professing a commitment to the rule of law, property rights, and equal justice. This contradiction is not merely a historical curiosity. It is a living wound at the heart of American democracy—a wound that festers in the poverty of Pine Ridge, in the contaminated water of Navajo Nation communities, in the missing and murdered Indigenous women whose cases go uninvestigated, and in the quiet despair of communities severed from the land that sustained them for millennia.

The remedy is not charity. It is not a gesture of goodwill or a symbolic acknowledgment of past wrongs. It is the fulfillment of legal obligations that were freely undertaken by the United States government and enshrined in the highest law of the land. It is the restoration of property to its rightful owners. It is the minimum required to bring American practice into alignment with American principle.

Land back is not a radical demand. It is a conservative one, in the deepest sense of the word: it asks the United States to conserve the rule of law, to honor its contracts, and to hold itself to the standards it imposes on everyone else. The question is not whether the United States can afford land restitution and reparations. The question is whether the United States can afford—legally, morally, or democratically—to continue pretending that the debt does not exist.

The treaties were signed. The promises were made. The land was stolen. Justice requires that it be returned.

  • Treaties carry constitutional weight. Under Article VI of the Constitution, treaties are "the supreme law of the land." Proponents argue that honoring them is not a special concession but a legal obligation.
  • Many removals violated existing agreements. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 led to forced relocations (notably the Trail of Tears) that contradicted prior treaty guarantees of territorial integrity.

Documented Historical Injustices

Proponents argue reparations address quantifiable, well-documented harms:

Land Dispossession

  • Native peoples held roughly 1.5 billion acres prior to European colonization. Today, tribal lands amount to approximately 56 million acres—about 2.3% of the U.S. land mass.
  • The Dawes Act (1887) alone resulted in the transfer of approximately 90 million acres from tribal to non-Native ownership through the allotment system.
  • The Indian Claims Commission (1946–1978) resolved hundreds of cases but typically paid pennies per acre based on historical land values, which critics describe as inadequate.

Cultural and Human Losses

  • Boarding school system: From the 1870s through the mid-20th century, the federal government operated or funded schools designed explicitly to eliminate Native languages and cultures. The Department of the Interior's 2022 investigative report identified over 400 such institutions and documented widespread abuse and deaths.
  • Population decline: From an estimated pre-contact population of 5–15 million (estimates vary by methodology), the Native population in the contiguous U.S. fell to approximately 237,000 by 1900, due to warfare, disease, forced removal, and deliberate policy.
  • Religious suppression: Native spiritual practices were formally banned under federal law until the American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978.
  • Resource extraction: Federal management of tribal trust assets has been documented as mismanaged. The Cobell v. Salazar settlement (2009) addressed over a century of federal mismanagement of individual Indian trust accounts, resulting in a $3.4 billion settlement.

Economic Consequences

  • Contemporary Native Americans experience poverty rates roughly double the national average (~25% vs. ~12%).
  • Reservation infrastructure deficits are substantial: lower rates of electricity, running water, broadband access, and healthcare access compared to national averages.
  • Proponents argue these disparities are direct, traceable consequences of dispossession rather than incidental.

Proposed Forms of Reparations

Proposals vary in scope and mechanism:

Land Return (Land Back)

  • Federal public lands: Some proposals focus on transferring federally managed public lands (national forests, BLM land) back to tribal management or ownership, particularly where those lands overlap with treaty-guaranteed territories.
  • Co-management arrangements: Models already exist, such as the Bears Ears Inter-Tribal Coalition's involvement in monument management, and the return of the Blue Lake sacred site to Taos Pueblo in 1970.
  • Practical argument: Proponents note that much of the land under discussion is not privately owned but federally held, reducing direct displacement concerns.

Financial Reparations

  • Direct payments, trust fund establishment, or investment in tribal infrastructure.
  • Funding for language revitalization, healthcare, education, and housing.
  • Restructuring or forgiving debts related to federal programs.

Policy and Governance Reforms

  • Strengthening tribal sovereignty and self-governance authority.
  • Reforming the federal trust relationship.
  • Restoring tribal jurisdiction over criminal and civil matters on tribal lands.

Supposed Benefits Cited by Proponents

Legal and Constitutional Consistency

  • Honoring treaties fulfills existing legal obligations rather than creating new ones.
  • Proponents argue it strengthens rule-of-law norms when governments honor their agreements.

Environmental Stewardship

  • Research published in journals such as Nature Sustainability and Environmental Science & Policy has found that indigenous-managed lands often show equal or greater biodiversity preservation compared to conventional protected areas.
  • Approximately 80% of the world's remaining biodiversity exists on indigenous lands, according to World Bank data.
  • Proponents argue land return could serve dual purposes of justice and conservation.

Economic Development

  • Greater tribal control over resources and governance could enable economic self-determination.
  • Existing examples: tribes that have gained greater sovereignty over their resources (such as certain gaming compacts or energy development agreements) have in some cases seen significant economic improvement.
  • Reduced federal dependency is often cited as a long-term goal.

Public Health Improvements

  • Addressing housing, water, and healthcare infrastructure gaps could reduce documented health disparities.
  • Cultural reconnection (language, land access, traditional practices) has been associated in public health literature with improved mental health outcomes, including reduced rates of suicide and substance abuse in indigenous communities.

Reconciliation and Social Cohesion

  • Proponents point to international models—such as New Zealand's Waitangi Tribunal process, Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, and Australia's native title framework—as examples where addressing indigenous claims contributed to broader national reconciliation (though all remain works in progress with their own criticisms).

Sovereignty and Self-Determination

  • Indigenous sovereignty is recognized in international law, including the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007), which the U.S. endorsed in 2010.
  • Proponents argue that meaningful sovereignty requires a land base and resource access sufficient for self-governance.

Existing Precedents

Several actions have already established partial precedent:

Action Year Details
Blue Lake return to Taos Pueblo 1970 48,000 acres of sacred land returned by Congress
Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act 1971 44 million acres and $963 million transferred
Maine Indian Claims Settlement 1980 $81.5 million for land purchase
Cobell Settlement 2009 $3.4 billion for trust mismanagement
Bears Ears co-management 2022 Tribal coalition given formal role in monument management

Complexity and Counterpoints Worth Noting

A neutral treatment should acknowledge that these proposals involve genuine complexities:

  • Competing land claims between tribes, states, private owners, and the federal government.
  • Implementation questions about which tribal governments receive what, how mixed-heritage individuals are included, and how overlapping historical claims are resolved.
  • Political feasibility remains a major barrier.
  • Scale and cost estimates vary enormously depending on the proposal.
  • Some tribal nations themselves differ on preferred approaches—some prioritize sovereignty reforms over financial transfers, or land return over cash settlements.

Summary

The core argument for reparations and land return rests on a documented historical record of treaty violations, legally recognized land seizures, deliberate cultural destruction, and measurable ongoing consequences. Proponents frame these not primarily as charity or progressive policy preference but as fulfillment of existing legal obligations and correction of documented governmental actions. The supposed benefits span legal consistency, environmental stewardship, economic development, public health, and alignment with international norms on indigenous rights—though significant practical and political challenges attend every proposed implementation path.

Let me close with this.

We live in a nation that celebrates the rule of law. That venerates the Constitution. That teaches its children about the sanctity of contracts and the principle that agreements must be honored.

Then honor them.

Three hundred and seventy treaties. Exposed violations. Exposed theft. Exposed violence. All of it documented. All of it acknowledged. None of it remedied.

The Native nations of this land have waited long enough. They have been patient beyond any reasonable expectation. They have fought in American wars, contributed to American culture, protected American lands, and endured American cruelty — and they are still here. Still sovereign. Still unbroken.

The question before us is not whether they deserve justice. That question was answered long ago. The question is whether we have the courage to deliver it.

I believe we do. I believe we must. And I believe the time is now.

Return the land. Fund the obligations. Restore the sovereignty. Honor the treaties.

It is not charity. It is not generosity. It is what is owed.

In the annals of American history, few chapters are as stained with betrayal and injustice as the treatment of Native American nations. These pacts explicitly delineated boundaries, reserved territories, and protected cultural practices. However, as American expansionism surged westward, these treaties became inconvenient obstacles. A prime example is the Treaty of Fort Laramie in 1868, which guaranteed the Lakota Sioux control over the Black Hills region—a sacred site rich in spiritual and material value. Just six years later, the discovery of gold prompted the U.S. Army's illegal incursion, leading to the Great Sioux War and the eventual Supreme Court ruling in United States v. The Sioux refused the paltry monetary compensation offered, demanding the land's return instead—a stance that highlights the inadequacy of financial remedies alone but underscores the treaty's enduring legal weight.

This pattern of perfidy extended far beyond isolated incidents. The Indian Removal Act of 1830, signed by President Andrew Jackson, forcibly relocated tens of thousands of Cherokee, Choctaw, and other southeastern tribes along the Trail of Tears, resulting in the deaths of at least 4,000 Cherokee alone. These removals contravened treaties like the Treaty of New Echota (1835), which the Cherokee Supreme Court had declared fraudulent. Will we choose the path of reckoning, justice, and restitution? Or will we continue to ignore the deep wounds of history?

I stand before you not just as an advocate, but as a voice for the countless Indigenous people whose ancestors were murdered, whose children were forced into boarding schools to erase their language and culture, and whose lands were taken through betrayal and bloodshed. The treaties that were signed with solemn handshakes and witnessed by the thunder of cannons were violated within decades. Promises made to our people—promises exchanged for what little land and resources were left to us—were shattered like glass.

Yet, even in the face of this suffering, our Nations persist. We hold onto our traditions, our stories, and our unyielding demand for justice. And today, I say clearly and unapologetically: It is time to return what was taken. It is time to make amends. It is time to restore Indigenous sovereignty.

The Case for Substantial Land Return

Land is not just an asset—it is the foundation of our identity, our spirituality, and our survival. When we speak of land return, we are not asking for charity. We are demanding the restoration of what was illegally seized—not just a few scattered acres, but significant territory that can sustain our people and our future.

Consider the Sioux Nation, whose Black Hills were stolen in violation of the Fort Laramie Treaty. Consider the Cherokees, forcibly marched on the Trail of Tears while their ancestral lands were handed to settlers. Consider the truths of the Dawes Act, which fractionalized our sovereignty and left generations in poverty. These are not ancient history—these are crimes whose consequences still blight our communities today.

A meaningful land return program must:

  • Acknowledge treaty violations and restore lands back to their original owners through federal, state, and corporate holdings.
  • Create a fair process where Native Nations have a direct say in which lands are returned, ensuring they are returned in usable, ecologically sustainable ways.
  • Incentivize corporations and institutions to cede land back to Indigenous stewardship, just as universities and churches have begun to reckon with their roles in theft and oppression.

The Moral and Financial Imperative of Reparations

Reparations are not a radical idea—they are a fundamental principle of justice. Every stolen acre, every broken treaty, every life lost demands compensation. Financial reparations must address:

  • Centuries of stolen labor—enslaved Indigenous people built railways, worked fields, and endured forced assimilation, yet their descendants live in poverty.
  • Cultural and generational trauma—the loss of language, spirituality, and family structures due to government policies must be accounted for.
  • Economic disparities—Native communities suffer the highest poverty rates in America, while corporations profit from resources taken from our lands.

A reparations fund must be substantial, structured, and long-term. It must fund:

  • Healthcare for our communities, which suffer from environmental racism and neglect.
  • Education in Native languages, history, and culture.
  • Infrastructure to ensure clean water, housing, and self-sustaining economies.

Restoring True Sovereignty

Reparations and land return must also come with a full acknowledgement of Indigenous sovereignty—something the U.S. government has consistently undermined. Federal recognition laws have been weaponized to disenfranchise tribes. Bureau of Indian Affairs policies have stripped communities of self-determination. This must end.

We must demand:

  • Federal policies that strengthen tribal self-governance, not impose restrictions.
  • Legal frameworks that recognize Indigenous laws and legal systems on returned lands.
  • A seat at the table in all decisions affecting Native Nations—no more top-down paternalism.

A Future Built on Justice

I know some will call this speech "divisive." They will say, "The past is the past." But justice is not division—justice is reconciliation. And the past is a crime we are living with today.

To every Native American listening: Your pain is seen. Your resilience is recognized. Your demands are just. And to those in power: We are no longer asking. We are demanding—in the same unbreakable spirit of our ancestors—"Give us back what is ours."

The time for empty apologies is over. The time for symbolic gestures is done. True justice requires bold action: Land. Reparations. Sovereignty.

Let history remember us not as those who stood by while injustice persisted, but as those who had the courage to make it right.

In the spirit of our ancestors, I say: Aho. Migwetch. Hóŋhe. Wah’Shah. Thank you.
